subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 writing task on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The writing process: plan, draft, edit and proofread
Vocabulary and sentence variety for effect

questions.q: The main purpose of a piece of writing is 'to persuade'. Which task is it most likely to be?
options: A recipe for a chocolate cake
A letter urging the council to build a skatepark
A short story about a haunted house
A report on last term's exam results
questions.explain: Persuading means changing what a reader thinks or does, so a letter urging action fits. A recipe instructs, a story entertains and a report informs.

questions.q: You are writing for young children learning to read. Which choice best suits that audience?
options: Long, complex sentences with subordinate clauses
Formal, technical vocabulary and passive verbs
Short sentences, simple words and a friendly tone
Slang, abbreviations and inside jokes
questions.explain: Young readers need short sentences, simple vocabulary and a warm tone. Complex sentences, technical words or slang would all be wrong for that audience.

questions.lo: The writing process: plan, draft, edit and proofread
questions.q: Which is the correct order of the writing process?
options: Draft, plan, proofread, edit
Plan, draft, edit, proofread
Proofread, edit, draft, plan
Edit, plan, draft, proofread
questions.explain: You plan your ideas first, draft them, edit to improve the writing, then proofread last to catch spelling and punctuation errors.

questions.lo: The writing process: plan, draft, edit and proofread
questions.q: During your final read-through you spot 'definately' and correct it to 'definitely'. Which stage is this?
options: Planning
Drafting
Editing
Proofreading
questions.explain: Proofreading is the last check for surface errors such as spelling and punctuation. Editing, by contrast, is about improving the ideas and wording.

questions.q: What is the job of a topic sentence?
options: To end the paragraph with a joke
To introduce the main idea of the paragraph
To list every fact you know
To correct the reader's grammar
questions.explain: A topic sentence states the paragraph's main idea; the rest of the paragraph then develops and explains it.

questions.q: In a story, when should you usually start a new paragraph?
options: After every single sentence
Only once, halfway through
When the time, place, topic or speaker changes
Never — stories should be one block
questions.explain: The TiPToP rule: begin a new paragraph when there is a change of Time, Place, Topic or Person (speaker). New speaker also means a new line in dialogue.

questions.q: "Solar power is clean. _______, it does not work at night." Which connective best fits the gap?
options: Therefore
However
For example
Firstly
questions.explain: The second idea contrasts with the first, so a contrasting connective ('However') signals the turn. 'Therefore' would wrongly suggest a cause-and-effect link.

questions.q: Which is the strongest opening line for a piece of descriptive writing about a storm?
options: In this piece I will describe a storm.
Storms are a type of weather event.
The sky cracked open and rain hammered the tin roof.
I am going to tell you all about storms now.
questions.explain: A vivid image with strong verbs ('cracked', 'hammered') hooks the reader instantly. The others announce the topic rather than dropping us into the scene.

questions.q: Why is "...and then I woke up and it was all a dream" usually a weak ending?
options: It uses too much vocabulary
It cancels out everything that happened, so it feels like a cheat
It is too short to be an ending
It contains a spelling mistake
questions.explain: The 'it was all a dream' ending undoes the story's events, leaving the reader feeling cheated. A stronger ending circles back to an earlier image or lands a punchy final line.

questions.lo: Vocabulary and sentence variety for effect
questions.q: Which verb choice is most precise and effective for: 'The old man ___ down the icy path.'?
options: went
shuffled
did move
was going
questions.explain: 'Shuffled' shows exactly how an old man moves on ice. 'Went', 'did move' and 'was going' are vague and add nothing to the picture.

questions.lo: Vocabulary and sentence variety for effect
questions.q: What is the main effect of placing a very short sentence after several long ones?
options: It confuses the reader
It creates emphasis and impact
It is a grammatical error
It makes the writing informal
questions.explain: Varying sentence length for effect is a key craft skill: a sudden short sentence after longer ones stands out and hits the reader with impact.

questions.q: Which sentence best 'shows' that a character is angry, rather than 'telling' us?
options: She was really, really angry.
She felt very angry inside.
She slammed the door so hard the windows rattled.
She was angry and cross and furious.
questions.explain: Showing uses an action or detail ('slammed the door... windows rattled') so the reader infers the emotion. The others simply state that she was angry.

questions.q: Which statement about 'show, don't tell' is correct?
options: You must never state anything plainly in any writing
It suits stories and description, where atmosphere matters
It means using as many adjectives as possible
It only applies to non-fiction reports
questions.explain: Showing works best where mood and emotion matter, such as stories and description. Reports and explanations often need clear, plain 'telling' instead.

questions.q: Which sentence is written in Standard English, suitable for a formal essay?
options: We was going to the shops when it happened.
They should of told us about the change.
I have not done anything wrong.
I ain't got no idea what you mean.
questions.explain: 'I have not done anything wrong' uses Standard English. The others contain non-standard forms: 'we was', 'should of' (should have) and a double negative.

questions.q: You are writing a formal complaint to a company. Which opening has the right register?
options: Oi, sort out my broken order asap!!
I am writing to express my dissatisfaction with a recent order.
hey so my thing didn't turn up lol
You lot are useless, give me my money back.
questions.explain: A formal complaint needs a polite, controlled register. The others use slang, text-speak or rudeness, which weakens the writing and the complaint.

questions.q: "After a long delay caused by heavy snow, the 8am train finally left the station at 11am." Which is the best one-line summary?
options: Snow is a common problem for trains in winter.
The 8am train was delayed by snow and left at 11am.
The train station was very busy that morning.
Passengers were angry about the long wait.
questions.explain: A good summary keeps the key facts (which train, the cause, the outcome) in fewer words. The others add opinion or information the text never gave.

questions.q: When you summarise a passage, what should you do?
options: Copy out the whole passage word for word
Add your own new opinions and examples
Keep the main points and drop the extra detail
Rewrite it in a longer, more detailed way
questions.explain: Summarising means capturing the main points in far fewer words, keeping the meaning but cutting supporting detail. You do not add new ideas or copy it all out.

questions.q: "Cleaner, greener and cheaper energy is within our reach." Which persuasive technique is used?
options: Rhetorical question
Rule of three (a triple)
Statistic
Alliteration only
questions.explain: Three linked ideas ('cleaner, greener and cheaper') form a rule of three, which makes the point memorable and rhythmic. There is no question or statistic here.

questions.q: Which technique is used in: "Do we really want our town to be remembered for its litter?"
options: A rhetorical question
A fact
Alliteration
A simile
questions.explain: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for a real answer, nudging the reader towards agreement. It is one of the most useful persuasive tools.

questions.q: Which is the best advice for using AFOREST persuasive techniques?
options: Use every technique in every sentence
Use them sparingly, so each one has real impact
Only ever use statistics
Avoid them completely in persuasive writing
questions.explain: Persuasive techniques work best used sparingly and deliberately. Cramming in every device at once feels forced and actually weakens the argument.
